name: PsyMI
tagline: Index of Open-Source Implementations of Psychoacoustic Metrics
description: An index of open-source implementations of psychoacoustic metrics (loudness, sharpness, roughness, fluctuation strength, tonality, impulsiveness and psychoacoustic annoyance), organised by the standard edition or model each implementation follows. All programming languages.
credit: Developed by Zhenxian LI with assistance from Claude Code.
ordering: Implementations and projects are listed by group: established, newly released, developing, legacy, others. Newly released projects were first released less than about a year ago and are not yet widely used in the community. Legacy projects are archived or have had no commit for three years or more; the most widely used projects (most_widely_used: true) and reference programs are never legacy. Within each group, projects that are still active and widely recognised come first. Projects in the others group do not compute the metrics themselves; they call another indexed project (listed in calls), and their rows appear under also_through instead of implementations.

standing.established: Described in a publication, used by others, or written by the authors of the model, with more than a year of history.
standing.newly-released: First released less than about a year ago, and not yet widely used in the community.
standing.developing: Public for more than a year, but without a publication or documented use by others: research, teaching or personal code.

group.established: Described in a publication, used by others, or written by the authors of the model, with more than a year of history.
group.newly-released: First released less than about a year ago, and not yet widely used in the community.
group.developing: Public for more than a year, but without a publication or documented use by others: research, teaching or personal code.
group.legacy: Archived, or no commit for three years or more. Kept for reference: the code may follow an older edition and may not run with current software.
group.others: Tools that do not compute the metrics themselves: interfaces, front ends and wrappers that call one of the indexed projects.

status.available: In the latest release, or on the default branch of a project without releases.
status.unreleased: Merged on the default branch but newer than the latest release.
status.proposed: Open pull request or separate branch, not merged.

validation.standard-data: Compared with test signals or values published in the standard or the model paper.
validation.reference-code: Compared with the reference program or the model authors' own code.
validation.self-tests: Tests exist, but without external reference data.
validation.not-stated: The project does not say how it was validated.

coverage.current: an available implementation of the current edition
coverage.new: an available implementation of the current edition, but only from newly released projects
coverage.partial: only unreleased, proposed or older-edition implementations

families.name: Loudness
families.summary: How loud a sound is perceived, in sone (loudness) and phon (loudness level). Four model families are standardised: Zwicker (ISO 532-1), Moore–Glasberg (ISO 532-2), Moore–Glasberg–Schlittenlacher (ISO 532-3) and the Sottek Hearing Model (ECMA-418-2).

families.name: Sharpness
families.summary: The sensation produced by high-frequency content, in acum. Standardised in DIN 45692 on top of Zwicker loudness; ECMA-418-2 does not define sharpness.

families.name: Roughness
families.summary: The sensation produced by fast amplitude or frequency modulation (roughly 15 to 300 Hz, strongest near 70 Hz), in asper.

families.name: Fluctuation strength
families.summary: The sensation produced by slow modulation (below about 20 Hz, strongest near 4 Hz), in vacil.

families.name: Tonality
families.summary: How prominent tonal components are. Covers psychoacoustic tonality models (Aures, ECMA-418-2) and the engineering measures used for product noise (tone-to-noise ratio, prominence ratio) and for environmental noise (tonal audibility and tone adjustments).

families.name: Impulsiveness
families.summary: How prominent impulsive sounds are, and the adjustment applied to them in environmental noise assessment.

families.name: Psychoacoustic annoyance
families.summary: Single-number models that combine loudness, sharpness, roughness, fluctuation strength and, in later models, tonality into a predicted annoyance.

families.name: Related quantities
families.summary: Quantities that psychoacoustic tools often include and that are closely tied to the metrics above.

methods.name: Zwicker loudness
methods.title: Zwicker loudness (ISO 532-1, DIN 45631)
methods.summary: Loudness from Zwicker's model: third-octave band levels are turned into specific loudness on the critical-band (Bark) scale and integrated. ISO 532-1:2017 specifies one procedure for stationary sounds and one for time-varying sounds (from which percentile values such as N5 are taken), and replaced method B of ISO 532:1975. The German standards DIN 45631 (stationary) and DIN 45631/A1 (time-varying) specify Zwicker's method; ISO 532-1:2017 states that its stationary method is based on DIN 45631:1991.
methods.notes: In China, GB/T 25982-2024 (interior noise of buses, in force since July 2025) sets loudness and sharpness limits and gives Zwicker's calculation in an informative annex.

edition_notes.iso-532-1975: Method B (Zwicker) for stationary sounds, from third-octave levels.
edition_notes.chalupper-fastl-2002: Dynamic loudness model built on Zwicker's model, also for hearing impairment (not standardised).
edition_notes.din-45631-a1-2010: Adds the procedure for time-varying sounds.
edition_notes.iso-532-1-2017: Stationary and time-varying procedures; Annex A reference program, Annex B test signals.
edition_notes.iso-532-1-ed2-draft: Second edition at committee-draft stage since November 2024.

implementations.note: Checked with the 25 test signals of Annex B.2–B.5 against the standard's tolerances. Fixes to the time-varying procedure are on `main` only (PR #48).

implementations.scope: stationary (also per segment and from a spectrum) and time-varying
implementations.note: Validation scripts use the ISO 532-1 Annex B test signals; the documentation marks it as validated.

A commit of 2017-12-11 says the code was verified with the time-varying test signals of Annex B.5; no check of the stationary method is stated. The header cites a 2014 draft of ISO 532-1 and describes the code as Ella Manor's 2015 MATLAB port, with adjustments, of the Annex A C code.
Also outputs loudness fluctuation and time-varying sharpness.

implementations.scope: stationary and time-varying; also from 28 third-octave levels
implementations.note: Model tables taken from MoSQITo and checked element by element; one upper-slope value (0.22) follows the ISO 532-1 reference C table where MoSQITo uses 0.24. Comparison results are not published.

Parity tests with MoSQITo 1.2.1 on nine synthetic and Annex B signals (worst reported difference 1.3e-9). Checked separately against ISO 532-1 Annex B: the README reports stationary offsets of about +0.82 % and −0.76 % for signals 3 and 5, inside the standard's tolerance, and details signals 3, 5 and 10 in docs/ISO-ANNEXB-NUMERICAL-ERROR-2026-07-04.md. Python uses the same names (`iso532.loudness_zwst` …); the C API has `iso532_loudness_zwst`, `iso532_loudness_zwtv` and `iso532_stream_*`.
Written from the Annex A reference program; Annex B test signals are used in the tests.
Compared with MoSQITo 1.2.1 on calibrated test signals, used as a development-time reference (`NOTES.md`, `tools/psycho_oracle`); no MoSQITo code is ported.
Checked against ISO 532-1 Annex B signal 1, the only 28-band reference in Annex B (83.296 sone, tolerance ±5 %), and per Bark bin against MoSQITo output (maximum difference below 0.001 sone/Bark).

implementations.scope: time-varying, from band levels at 2000 Hz; N5 and N10
implementations.note: Stages are tested against MoSQITo `loudness_zwtv` intermediates (agreement about 1e-9 to 1e-15). An Annex B.4 "Test signal 6" test regenerates band levels from a local MoSQITo checkout and is skipped when none is present; CI clones MoSQITo for it. The ISO WAV files are not included.
Compared with SQAT (MATLAB).

implementations.scope: stationary and time-varying, from third-octave levels
implementations.note: The file header says "Loudness ISO 532-1:2014" and the filter coefficients are labelled "ISO 532-1:2014"; the published edition is ISO 532-1:2017.
The analyser names J. Chalupper and H. Fastl as authors.

Tested against "a quick and dirty Python port of the Matlab code private by GENESIS ACOUSTICS". Uses 28 third-octave filters with third-order Butterworth responses after ANSI S1.11:1986; there is no time-varying (DIN 45631/A1) model.
Port of the 1991 BASIC program "according to DIN 45631 (ISO 532B)", the program that accompanies DIN 45631:1991; the same program is the basis of deeuu/loudness.

also_through.scope: stationary, from a waveform or WAV file
also_through.note: Computes the third-octave levels itself (per-band Butterworth filters of order 3 by default, as in MoSQITo) and passes them to ZwickerLoudness.jl for the loudness. ISO 532-1 Annex B signals 2–5, synthesised in-process, are within the standard's ±5 % (+2.9 %, +3.6 %, +0.5 % and +2.6 % per the README).

also_through.scope: time-varying, from a waveform or WAV file at 48 kHz
also_through.note: Cross-checked end to end with MoSQITo `loudness_zwtv` (N(t) about 3e-16 relative, N5/N10 about 2e-15 absolute), plus an Annex B.4 test that is skipped when the ISO recording is not available locally. The Annex A filter cascade is transcribed from MoSQITo (`_third_octave_levels`, `_square_and_smooth`).

methods.name: Moore–Glasberg loudness
methods.title: Moore–Glasberg loudness of stationary sounds (ISO 532-2, ANSI S3.4)
methods.summary: Loudness of stationary sounds from the Moore–Glasberg model: the spectrum is turned into an excitation pattern on the ERB-number scale, then into specific loudness, which is summed. ANSI S3.4-2007 standardised the model of Moore, Glasberg & Baer (1997) with later modifications; ISO 532-2:2017 specifies the method for monaural and binaural listening.

edition_notes.moore-1997: Model paper (thresholds, loudness and partial loudness).
edition_notes.ansi-s3-4-2007: American standard based on the 1997 model with later modifications.
edition_notes.chen-2011: Faster excitation-pattern calculation, also for hearing loss (not standardised).
edition_notes.iso-532-2-2017: Monaural and binaural loudness of stationary sounds; source code supplied with the standard.
edition_notes.iso-532-2-ed2-draft: Second edition at committee-draft stage since November 2024.

implementations.note: Listed as "CHEN2011 - Fast excitation pattern estimation"; experiment script `exp_chen2011`.
Listed as "MOORE1997 - Loudness model for stationary signals" in models/Contents.m. AMT's experiment scripts (`exp_…`) reproduce published results; this model has `exp_moore1997`.

implementations.scope: one channel, or two channels for binaural loudness
implementations.note: Version 1.02 (27 October 2015). Two-channel input gives binaural loudness after Moore & Glasberg (2007). The audio is resampled to 32 kHz.
The documentation says it reproduces the Annex B tone and broadband cases to within a percent or two.

The implementation document says the model is compared with the results shown in the original article (plots of its Fig. 8 and Fig. 12). Numerical error reports (PDF) compare intermediate arrays, such as the outer- and middle-ear filter, with AMT's MATLAB output.

implementations.scope: with the binaural inhibition of Moore & Glasberg (2007) for two ears
implementations.note: Unit tests cover each module and model. A validation script writes computed and expected loudness of pure tones to CSV; the expected values are labelled "Table 7" and "Example 2" without naming their source.

Also cites Glasberg & Moore (1990) for the auditory filters. The analyser description says it covers time-varying and binaural loudness, and it also cites Glasberg & Moore (2002) and Moore & Glasberg (2007).

methods.name: Time-varying loudness (Moore–Glasberg–Schlittenlacher)
methods.title: Time-varying loudness, Moore–Glasberg–Schlittenlacher (ISO 532-3)
methods.summary: Loudness of time-varying sounds as instantaneous, short-term and long-term loudness. It starts from the Glasberg & Moore (2002) model; Moore et al. (2016) added binaural inhibition and Moore et al. (2018) revised the time constants. ISO 532-3:2023 standardises the resulting Moore–Glasberg–Schlittenlacher method for stationary and time-varying sounds.

edition_notes.glasberg-moore-2002: Time-varying loudness model (short-term and long-term loudness).
edition_notes.iso-532-3-2023: Standardised method; source code supplied with the standard.
edition_notes.iso-532-3-ed2-draft: Second edition at committee-draft stage since November 2024.

implementations.scope: reference MATLAB code referred to in ISO 532-3, per its readme
implementations.note: Written by the model's authors (per the readme PDF). The folder "code for tables" has scripts that compute Table 5 (sone to phon) and the values of Annexes B and C (AnnexC.m is headed "Signals numbered as in ISO 532-2 Annex B"); the scripts do not name ISO 532-3.
Listed as "MOORE2016 - Binaural loudness model"; there is no `exp_moore2016` experiment script on the develop branch.
Listed as "GLASBERG2002 - Loudness model for time-variant signals"; experiment script `exp_glasberg2002`.

implementations.scope: time-varying; one channel, or two channels for binaural loudness
implementations.note: Same function as the stationary model; the binaural extension follows Moore & Glasberg (2007).
Documented deviations: it runs at the native sample rate instead of resampling to 32 kHz, and the Annex B WAV-file cases are not reproduced (Annex C values are used instead).
Described as a "1:1 port" of AMT `moore2016`, with outer and middle ear per ANSI S3.4-2007 (docstring); agreement with AMT is claimed in the documentation, without stored reference data.
Present in the code but not described in the implementation document.
Ported from AMT `glasberg2002`; agreement with AMT is claimed in the documentation, without stored reference data.

implementations.scope: instantaneous, short-term and long-term loudness; binaural
implementations.note: Tests run in GitHub Actions compare overall loudness, the first five short-term and long-term values and selected intermediate stages for one input (1 kHz tone, 100 ms, 32 kHz) with hard-coded expected values. The README calls this "a known accurate output", but neither it nor the tests say where the values come from.

Per the header, excitation patterns follow ANSI S3.4-2007, and parameter sets use the modified long-term time constants of Moore et al. (2003) and the ANSI S3.4-2007 equation for specific loudness at high levels.
The same analyser as the stationary entry; its description cites Glasberg & Moore (2002).

methods.name: Sottek Hearing Model loudness
methods.title: Loudness from the Sottek Hearing Model (ECMA-418-2)
methods.summary: Loudness from the Sottek Hearing Model defined in ECMA-418-2. The hearing model (Clause 5) produces specific loudness; the 2nd edition (2022) added a loudness calculation for sounds with tonal and noise components (Clause 8). ECMA-418-2 has had four editions in five years, so implementations of different editions can disagree.

edition_notes.ecma-418-2-ed2: New Clause 8, loudness of sounds with subcritical or wider bandwidth.
edition_notes.ecma-418-2-ed3: Adds a diffuse-field outer and middle ear filter.
edition_notes.ecma-418-2-ed4: Hearing-model clauses 5.1.2.2 and 5.1.5.2 revised; conformance requires 48 kHz sampling.

implementations.scope: MATLAB and Python; binaural and specific loudness
implementations.note: MATLAB and Python verified against HEAD acoustics ArtemiS v17.1 for a 1 kHz tone at 40 dB SPL, a 1 kHz tone amplitude-modulated at 70 Hz at 60 dB SPL and a 30 s binaural street recording; the audio and reference results are on Zenodo (doi:10.5281/zenodo.18849587).

implementations.scope: mono or stereo, with combined binaural output
implementations.note: Unit tests check the standard's calibration signals (1 kHz, 40 dB gives 1 sone_HMS); the MATLAB code it was translated from was compared with commercial reference software in the paper.
Updated to the 4th edition on `main` in 2025.

implementations.scope: mono or two channels with binaural combination
implementations.note: Checked against equal-loudness contours and against reference results from commercial software on a binaural recording.

implementations.scope: Clause 5 hearing-model specific and total loudness only; the Clause 8 loudness added in the 2nd edition is not implemented
implementations.note: Followed the 1st edition (2020) in versions 1.0.0–1.1.1 and the 2nd edition (2022) from 1.2.0. Validation scripts compare with figures of the standard.

implementations.scope: Clause 8 loudness with tonal/noise separation; mono or stereo
implementations.note: Adapted from the SQAT/RefMap MATLAB code by Lotinga and Torjussen. Comparison results are not published.
Checked at the calibration signal only, where it gives 0.9843 sone_HMS (−1.55 %).

implementations.scope: hearing model with specific and total loudness
implementations.note: Validation scripts compare the ear filter and model output with figures and values from ECMA-418-2 and ECMA-74 Annex F; module `mosqito.functions.hearing_model`.

also_through.note: Compared by validation/FINAL_VAL.py with the bundled SQAT v1.3 MATLAB code, which follows ECMA-418-2:2024 (3rd edition), so the comparison crosses editions.

methods.name: Sharpness
methods.title: Sharpness (DIN 45692, Aures, von Bismarck)
methods.summary: Sharpness is the weighted first moment of specific loudness along the critical-band rate, with a weighting that emphasises high frequencies. DIN 45692:2009 standardises the weighting and a test procedure, using Zwicker specific loudness (ISO 532-1 / DIN 45631). Most implementations also offer the weightings of von Bismarck (1974) and Aures (1985).

edition_notes.aures-1985-euphony: Weighting that depends on total loudness.
edition_notes.fastl-zwicker-2007: Zwicker & Fastl weighting as given in the textbook.
edition_notes.din-45692-2009: Standardised weighting and test procedure; no revision announced.

implementations.scope: DIN 45692 weighting, plus von Bismarck and Aures options
implementations.note: Checked with the narrowband and broadband test signals of DIN 45692.

implementations.scope: weightings: DIN 45692, Aures, von Bismarck, Fastl
implementations.note: Validation scripts use the DIN 45692 test signals; the documentation marks it as validated.

implementations.scope: DIN 45692 weighting applied to ECMA-418-2 loudness
implementations.note: The DIN 45692 weighting is the option `widmann`; Aures (the default) and von Bismarck weightings are also offered. DIN 45692 itself is defined on Zwicker specific loudness. A further variant works from a Zwicker-based quasi-loudness (`acousticSharpFromQuasiLoud`). An inaccuracy in the Aures weighting was fixed on 2026-09-18.
The header describes a weighting fitted to data in Zwicker & Fastl's *Psychoacoustics: Facts and Models* (edition not stated), names the method "Fastl (1991)" and credits Claire Churchill (2004).

implementations.scope: also the informative Aures and von Bismarck variants
implementations.note: Checked with the DIN 45692 reference signal and Tables A.2 and A.3.
Compared with MoSQITo 1.2.1 (tolerance ±5 %).
Compared with SQAT (MATLAB).
The file header says "Sharpness DIN 45692"; the function also returns the von Bismarck and Aures variants.

also_through.note: Calls `sharpness_din_st` of MoSQITo 1.2.1 with the DIN weighting.
Calls `sharpness_din_from_loudness`, `sharpness_din_perseg` or `sharpness_din_tv`; the weighting can be chosen.

methods.name: Roughness (Daniel & Weber)
methods.title: Roughness, Daniel & Weber model
methods.summary: Roughness from the model of Daniel & Weber (1997), an optimised version of Aures's (1985) model. It is not standardised, and the paper leaves details open (filter bank, calibration, framing), so implementations can give different values for the same signal.
methods.notes: SQAT rewrote its implementation in September 2026 (PR #65). It builds on Alejandro Osses's code and was corrected against revised code that Dik Hermes provided in 2025, which changes results compared with SQAT v1.3 and earlier.

edition_notes.aures-1985-roughness: Earlier model that Daniel & Weber optimised.

implementations.note: Checked against amplitude- and frequency-modulation dependences from the literature. Rewritten on `main` (PR #65, 2026-09-08) after revised code from Dik Hermes: 63 of 119 validation values go up and 56 down (largest change 0.155 asper).
The documentation marks it as validated against reference data.
Ported from PsySound3's `@RoughnessDW` by Ella Manor and Densil Cabrera (2015).
Follows SQAT revision `e6228b78`, which includes SQAT's September 2026 rewrite but not its later fix to the Terhardt filter bank (PR #77). Comparison results are not published.
Compared with MoSQITo 1.2.1 with a wider tolerance (±15 %); the README notes that published Daniel & Weber implementations differ by about 10–20 %.
Compared with SQAT v1.3, before SQAT's September 2026 rewrite.
Adapted for PsySound3 by Matt Flax (2006), with changes by Farhan Rizwi (2007). AARAE's `RoughnessDW.m` is a port of this analyser.

methods.name: Sottek Hearing Model roughness
methods.title: Roughness from the Sottek Hearing Model (ECMA-418-2)
methods.summary: Roughness from the Sottek Hearing Model, Clause 7 of ECMA-418-2. The 2nd edition (2022) added an optional entropy weighting for cases where rotational speed is measured; the 3rd edition (2024) adapted zero-padding and segmentation, and its refinements were mainly to roughness.

edition_notes.ecma-418-2-ed3: Zero-padding and segmentation adapted; refinements mainly to roughness.
edition_notes.ecma-418-2-ed4: Hearing-model and conformance updates (48 kHz sampling).

implementations.note: Verified against HEAD acoustics ArtemiS v17.1 with the same three signals as loudness.
Amended to the 4th edition on `main` in November 2025.
The documentation still lists it as under development. An open pull request (#95) fixes the low-pass filter range, which caused discrepancies with SQAT for time-varying signals.

implementations.scope: mono or stereo; optional entropy weighting not applied
implementations.note: Uses the standard's 20 ms grid and nominal calibration factor, where SQAT uses a slightly adjusted calibration. Comparison results are not published.
Checked at the calibration signal only.

also_through.note: Compared by validation/FINAL_VAL.py with the bundled SQAT v1.3 MATLAB code, which follows ECMA-418-2:2024 (3rd edition), so the comparison crosses editions.
Calls `roughness_ecma` of MoSQITo 1.2.1, whose bibliography cites ECMA-418-2:2022.

methods.name: Roughness (DIN 38455)
methods.title: Roughness, DIN 38455
methods.summary: DIN 38455:2024 is the first German standard for calculating roughness. Its text is not freely available, and the model it specifies could not be confirmed from public sources; a hearing-model roughness was proposed for DIN standardisation by Sottek & Becker (2019).

methods.name: Fluctuation strength (Osses et al.)
methods.title: Fluctuation strength, Osses et al. model and Fastl & Zwicker formula
methods.summary: Fluctuation strength describes slow modulation around 4 Hz. Osses, García & Kohlrausch (2016) proposed a signal-based model; Fastl & Zwicker give a closed-form expression for modulated tones and noises. Neither is standardised. ECMA-418-2:2025 added a hearing-model method, listed on its own page.

edition_notes.fastl-zwicker-2007: Closed-form expression for amplitude- and frequency-modulated sounds.

implementations.note: Checked against amplitude- and frequency-modulation dependences from the literature.
Compared with Table 1 of Osses et al. (2016) and with SQAT (correlation 0.98). Validated for amplitude modulation only; a steady 1 kHz tone reads about 0.09 vacil.
A conformance row checks Eq. (10.2) of Fastl & Zwicker for amplitude-modulated broadband noise.
`demos/demo_osses2016a.m` reproduces the figures of the paper with the included stimuli (AM and FM tones, AM noise and excerpts of real sounds).
The header cites Zwicker & Fastl, "Psychoacoustics: Facts and Models", without naming an edition.

methods.name: Sottek Hearing Model fluctuation strength
methods.name_zh: Sottek 听觉模型波动强度（ECMA-418-2）
methods.title: Fluctuation strength from the Sottek Hearing Model (ECMA-418-2)
methods.summary: Fluctuation strength from the Sottek Hearing Model, new in the 4th edition of ECMA-418-2 (June 2025, Clause 9). It uses high-resolution spectral analysis for modulation rates of about 0.25 to 20 Hz.

implementations.scope: needs at least 1.37 s of signal; binaural option
implementations.note: Merged on 2026-09-18. A draft report compares it with the MATLAB version (equal to floating-point precision) and with HEAD ArtemiS SUITE v17 (calibration 0.994 vs 1.003 vacil_HMS; recordings −8 % to +12 %). Five departures from the printed text are documented (four equations and one interpretation of Section 9.1.8).
Open pull request since 2026-09-17.
Checked at the calibration signal only (0.993 vacil_HMS); misprints found in Clause 9 are listed in its errata.

methods.name: Tonality (Aures)
methods.title: Tonality, Aures/Terhardt model
methods.summary: Tonality from Aures (1985): tonal components are extracted with the method of Terhardt, Stoll & Seewann (1982), weighted, and related to the loudness of the whole sound. Not standardised.
methods.notes: SQAT corrected several issues in September 2026 (for example, the level excess of only one tonal component, the last positive one, entered the result, combined with the first component's frequency and bandwidth), which changes results compared with SQAT v1.3 and earlier.

edition_notes.terhardt-1982: Extraction of tonal components used by the model.

implementations.note: v1.3 is checked with one signal-to-noise comparison. Eight defects were fixed on `main` in September 2026 (for example, only one tonal component's level excess entered the result, and tones were removed from the wrong spectrum), with new checks against Aures's Figs. 5 and 6.
Pull request from April 2026 following the improved Aures metric of Estreder et al. (2023); no maintainer reply.
Follows SQAT's September 2026 revision (250 ms Hann windows, 125 ms hop); exact agreement with MATLAB is not established. Comparison results are not published.
A June 2026 commit corrected its calibration; it predates SQAT's September 2026 fixes.

methods.name: Sottek Hearing Model tonality
methods.title: Tonality from the Sottek Hearing Model (ECMA-418-2)
methods.summary: Psychoacoustic tonality from the Sottek Hearing Model, Clause 6 of ECMA-418-2, with specific tonality and tonal frequency over time. The method came from ECMA-74 (17th edition, 2019) when ECMA-418-2 was first published in 2020.

edition_notes.ecma-74-ed17: Hearing model and tonality before ECMA-418-2 existed.
edition_notes.ecma-418-2-ed3: Diffuse-field outer and middle ear filter added (affects all metrics); refinements mainly to roughness.
edition_notes.ecma-418-2-ed4: Hearing-model and conformance updates (48 kHz sampling).

implementations.note: Verified against HEAD acoustics ArtemiS v17.1 with the same three signals as loudness.
Optional experimental tonal-annoyance weighting (Sottek & Becker, 2019) since 0.1.14.
A verification against Annex B.2 (PR #79) was merged and reverted on 2026-09-21 because the Annex B values of the 2025 edition appear to be out of date.
Comparison results are not published.
Checked at the calibration signal only.

also_through.note: Compared by validation/FINAL_VAL.py with the bundled SQAT v1.3 MATLAB code, which follows ECMA-418-2:2024 (3rd edition), so the comparison crosses editions.

methods.name: Tone-to-noise ratio and prominence ratio
methods.title: Tone-to-noise ratio and prominence ratio (ECMA-418-1)
methods.summary: Tone-to-noise ratio (TNR) and prominence ratio (PR) decide whether a discrete tone is prominent: TNR compares the tone with the noise in its critical band, PR compares the critical band with its neighbours. ECMA-418-1 took the method over from Annex D of ECMA-74 in 2020; its 3rd edition (2024) revised the TNR procedure.

edition_notes.ecma-418-1-ed1: Based on, and mostly identical to, ECMA-74 Annex D.
edition_notes.ecma-418-1-ed2: Maximum tone bandwidth for TNR set to 15 % of the critical band; corrections.
edition_notes.ecma-418-1-ed3: TNR procedure revised for repeatable results across FFT resolutions; terms rewritten.

implementations.note: Docstrings say "ECMA 418-1" without an edition; the helper code and the bibliography cite ECMA-74 Annex D (17th edition, 2019). The documentation marks it as available but not validated.
The "prominent" flag applies the numeric criterion only.
The README lists TNR/PR as available but not validated; the tests use synthetic tones in white noise.

methods.name: Tonal components (DIN 45681)

notes: Releases are published as downloads on SourceForge (`amtoolbox` and `amtoolbox-full`); the git repository's default branch is `develop`. The SourceForge project page mentions no GitHub or GitLab mirror.
Also contains `bramslow2004`, a loudness model considering hearing loss (AUDMOD), with the experiment script `exp_bramslow2004`; it has no reference entry in this index.
Neither the develop branch nor release 1.6.0 has a roughness, fluctuation strength, sharpness, tonality or annoyance model (`osses2021` is a monaural perceptual-similarity model).

Python ports of some of its loudness models exist: [torch_amt](https://github.com/StefanoGiacomelli/torch_amt) (`glasberg2002`, `moore2016`) and [NumpyLibforPsychoAcoustic](https://github.com/Ryrybros/NumpyLibforPsychoAcoustic) (`moore1997`, `glasberg2002`). There is no official Python package (amtoolbox and pyamtoolbox are not on PyPI).
The validation entries rest on AMT's design: each `exp_…` script is meant to reproduce figures of the model paper. The scripts' output was not checked for this index.

implements.note: Listed as "MOORE1997 - Loudness model for stationary signals" in models/Contents.m. AMT's experiment scripts (`exp_…`) reproduce published results; this model has `exp_moore1997`.
Listed as "CHEN2011 - Fast excitation pattern estimation"; experiment script `exp_chen2011`.
Listed as "GLASBERG2002 - Loudness model for time-variant signals"; experiment script `exp_glasberg2002`.
Listed as "MOORE2016 - Binaural loudness model"; there is no `exp_moore2016` experiment script on the develop branch.

projects.name: MoSQITo

Widely used, but without a release or a commit since April 2024.

paper.citation: San Millán-Castillo, R., Latorre-Iglesias, E., Glesser, M., Wanty, S., Jiménez-Caminero, D., & Álvarez-Jimeno, J. M. (2021). MOSQITO: an open-source and free toolbox for sound quality metrics in the industry and education. *INTER-NOISE 2021*, INCE Conference Proceedings 263(5), 1164–1175.

notes: Started by EOMYS in 2020. The default branch is `master`; its last commit and the last release (1.2.1) are both from 2024-04-22.
The documentation lists Soundscapy as a user; several other projects (PsychoBox, Sonemeter and others) wrap it.
Also computes the ANSI S3.5 speech intelligibility index (`sii_ansi`), which is outside the scope of this index.

Open, unanswered pull requests add Aures tonality ([#97](https://github.com/Eomys/MoSQITo/pull/97), 2026), ECMA-418-2 roughness fixes ([#95](https://github.com/Eomys/MoSQITo/pull/95), 2026) and an ISO 1996-2 Annex K tone detector ([#52](https://github.com/Eomys/MoSQITo/pull/52), 2022).
A C#/.NET port, Mosqito.NET, was announced in issue [#98](https://github.com/Eomys/MoSQITo/issues/98) (not checked).
The documentation lists hearing-model tonality (citing ECMA-74) as under development; there is no function for it.
caveats: No maintainer has answered issues or pull requests opened since 2024, including bug reports on TNR/PR (#80,
`import mosqito` fails when matplotlib is not installed, because it is imported but not declared as a dependency ([#100](https://github.com/Eomys/MoSQITo/issues/100)); install matplotlib yourself.
Its ECMA-418-2 functions follow the 2nd edition (2022), two editions behind the current one.

projects.summary: Pure Data library of psychoacoustic objects (C externals and abstractions) from the author's research on dissonance models. Includes ISO 226:2003 equal-loudness contours and phon, sone and dB conversions, as well as roughness, sharpness and tonalness objects.

paper.citation: Porres, A. T. (2011). Dissonance Model Toolbox in Pure Data. *Proceedings of the 4th Pure Data International Convention (PdCon11)*, Berlin.

notes: The roughness objects (`[roughness]`, `[roughcurve]`) compute the sensory dissonance of a spectrum given as lists of frequencies and amplitudes, with a model "derived from the work of Parncutt, Sethares, Vassilakis & Barlow"; this is not one of the signal-based roughness methods in this index.
`[sharpness~]` is an abstraction built on `[barks~]` (24 Bark bands) and names no sharpness model.
Tonalness, pitch salience and commonality follow Parncutt & Strasburger (1994), after Terhardt; they are not tonality metrics in the sense of this index.
From the author's MSc and PhD work (2005–2012). Version 1.1 was released on 2025-10-14 (git tags 1.0 of 2019 and 1.1; no GitHub releases). It builds with pd-lib-builder.

projects.name: iso532-3 (tv2018.m)
projects.license_note: No licence file. The readme PDF says: "The code is provided free for any research purposes. For commercial use please contact Brian C. J. Moore."
projects.summary: MATLAB code by Brian C. J. Moore, Brian R. Glasberg and Josef Schlittenlacher (Cambridge Hearing Group) for the loudness of time-varying sounds: the model of Moore et al. (2016) with the revised time constants of Moore et al. (2018). Its readme calls `tv2018.m` "the reference Matlab code referred to in ISO 532-3".
notes: There is no README.md; the documentation is the PDF "readme TVL 2018", which includes a worked example with the file 1k100ms.wav.

Takes a WAV file or a MATLAB variable with one or two channels and resamples it to 32 kHz. Outer- and middle-ear transfer functions for free-field, diffuse-field and eardrum presentation are included. Returns short-term and long-term loudness and the instantaneous loudness of each ear.
Also contains sone/phon conversion functions for the TV2015 and TV2018 tables (`Phon2SoneTV2015`, `Sone2PhonTV2015`, `Phon2SoneTV2018`, `Sone2PhonTV2018`).
The Python project LoudnessModel is a translation of the Cambridge MATLAB code for the same model.
caveats: The code was last changed in October 2021, before ISO 532-3 was published (July 2023); the readme refers to "ISO 532-3 (2021)". Whether it is identical to the source code supplied with the published standard is not stated.
For its text-file output, `tv2018.m` converts sone to phon with `Sone2PhonTV2015`, although TV2018 conversion tables were added in October 2021.
The WAV files that the Annex B script reads are not in the repository, and no computed tables are stored.

updates.title: First public version of PsyMI
updates.body:
PsyMI, the Psychoacoustic Metrics Index, starts with 32 projects in Python, MATLAB, Octave, C, C++, Rust,
Julia and Pure Data, and 22 methods from Zwicker loudness to aural detectability. Every implementation is
tied to the standard edition or model paper it follows, with links to the documentation the facts were taken
from. Repository dates, releases and package versions are refreshed once a month.

Worth knowing as of today:

- ECMA-418-2 is at its 4th edition (June 2025), which added fluctuation strength. sottek-hearing-model and
  refmap-psychoacoustics follow it, as do phonometry and MetaSona, two newly released projects that are not yet
  widely used. SQAT has it on its main branch only, and MoSQITo still follows the 2nd edition (2022).
- SQAT's latest release (v1.3) is licensed for non-commercial use only. Its main branch is GPL-3.0 and
  carries unreleased fixes to ISO 532-1 time-varying loudness, Aures tonality and Daniel & Weber roughness
  that change results.
- All three parts of ISO 532 are being revised; committee drafts have existed since November 2024.
- No open implementation was found for DIN 38455:2024 (the first German roughness standard), DIN 45681 or
  ISO/TS 20065:2022.
- Six projects disclose that AI tools assisted their development; each project page says where.
- Every project is in one group: established, newly released (first released less than about a year ago and
  not yet widely used), developing, legacy (archived, or no commit for three years) or others (calls another
  indexed project). Lists follow this order, so a new, little-used or unmaintained project is never the first
  suggestion.
- Candidates that could not be checked yet, such as PsyTools (TU Graz) and the ITA-Toolbox, are listed on
  the About page as leads.
